newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge accuses PM of coup plot amid tension.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge accuses PM of coup plot amid tension.

text.p: Cambodia's Khmer Rouge guerrillas on Friday accused the country's second prime minister of plotting a coup against his partner in Cambodia's fractured coalition as negotiations with the rebel group appeared stalled.

Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, who has been pushing controversial talks with the guerrillas, travelled to Bangkok on Friday to meet a senior Cambodian official, a key negotiator with the rebels, at Phnom Penh's embassy in Bangkok, a Thai security source said.

Ranariddh's top military adviser, another key negotiator in the Khmer Rouge talks, was sent to the guerrillas' northwest base of Anlong Veng on Thursday but he later reported no progress in securing the handover of reviled Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot, a key condition in peace talks with the government.

Relations between Ranariddh and Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, strained for more than a year over a power-sharing dispute, have been inflamed by a sharp difference over how to handle the dwindling Khmer Rouge rebel movement.

While Ranariddh has supported peace talks, Hun Sen considers negotiations with the rebels illegal. Political analysts said their dispute over the Khmer Rouge reflected attempts by both men to bolster their political positions ahead of elections next May.
The coalition government was formed after United Nations-run elections in 1993.

The rebels' clandestine radio, for years its main propaganda mouthpiece, said on Friday Hun Sen was building up troops and fire power in the capital and at his Tuol Krasang compound near Phnom Penh in preparation for a strike against Ranariddh.

Khmer Rouge radio is controlled by guerrillas loyal to the group's political leader, Khieu Samphan, who, along with other senior rebel figures, broke with Pol Pot last month and detained him at their Anlong Veng base.
"Around and in Phnom Penh, Hun Sen is increasing his armed troops and heavy weapons and has put his base of Tuol Krasang on high alert," said the radio, monitored in Phnom Penh.
"This event shows clearly...Hun Sen is preparing to make a coup d'etat by military means to fight and oust Ranariddh and his FUNCINPEC party from the government," it said.

But the Khmer Rouge failed to broadcast a statement demanded by Ranariddh, who said negotiations cannot move forward until the rebels declare they have broken with Pol Pot and recognise the kingdom's constitution.

Tension has been high in Phnom Penh for days following troop movements around the capital and a clash on Wednesday between armed forces units loyal to the rival premiers near a naval base 30 km (20 miles) north of Phnom Penh, which left several soldiers wounded and at least one dead.
Military officials said on Friday there were no further reports of clashes, but officials loyal to Hun Sen accused Ranariddh's men of planning troop movements towards the capital.

Adding to the general feeling of unease was news that both Ranariddh and Hun Sen and their families were out of the country, and rumours that senior members of Ranariddh's party were also planning foreign trips.
Ranariddh's office said he was travelling to France for a rest but Thai security sources said the prince was still in Bangkok late on Friday as he had been unable to meet his negotiator.

The negotiator, Long Sarin, later told Reuters he was on a trip to the northeastern Thai province of Surin, which borders an area of Cambodia controlled by forces loyal to Ranariddh, and had been unable to meet the prince.
Aides to Hun Sen said he was abroad but declined to say where, or why, he went. He was due back by Saturday, they said.
